heard: Voyager 2 launched two weeks before its twin, yet was named second. Most people naturally assume the lower-numbered spacecraft went up first. In 1977, NASA relied on a rare planetary alignment occurring once every 176 years. Voyager 1 took a shorter and faster trajectory, reaching Jupiter and Saturn sooner. Meanwhile, the truly first-launched probe simply took a much slower path. That brilliant cosmic detour made Voyager 2 the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune. It discovered hidden rings and dozens of new moons before diving completely south into interstellar space. That is precisely why Voyager 2 launched two weeks before its twin, yet was named second.
